title: The Transistor and Computing
content:
In 1947, John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley at Bell Labs demonstrated the transistor - a tiny solid-state switch and amplifier made from semiconductor material. It replaced the bulky, hot, fragile vacuum tube and became the fundamental building block of all modern electronics.

Why it mattered: a transistor can switch between on and off, representing the 1s and 0s of binary logic. Pack enough of them together and you can build circuits that compute.

The integrated circuit (late 1950s, Jack Kilby and Robert Noyce) put many transistors on a single chip of silicon. From there, progress followed what became known as Moore's Law: the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubled every couple of years for decades. Chips went from a handful of transistors to billions.

Consequences:
- Computers shrank from room-sized machines to devices that fit in a pocket.
- Cost per unit of computing power fell astronomically, putting computers in homes, cars, appliances, and phones.
- Entire industries - software, the internet, mobile communication, automation - rest on cheap, abundant transistors.

The transistor is arguably the most manufactured object in human history. The information age is, at its foundation, the story of learning to make these switches smaller, faster, cheaper, and more numerous than any technology before.
